raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 14-year-old boy from Rawalpindi, Pakistan, was admitted in July 2002 to Combined Military Hospital, Rawalpindi, with a 7-day history of a high fever (>38 C) and vomiting. He had relative bradycardia (heart rate 84 bpm) and a soft palpable spleen. His total leukocyte count was 3 x 109/L. Malarial parasites were not seen on examination of thin and thick smears of peripheral blood. The results of a routine urinalysis and chest radiographs were normal. A blood Widal test showed a titer of 320 against "O" (somatic) antigen of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi. Blood culture yielded the growth of Salmonella Typhi. The isolate was found to be resistant to the conventional antityphoid drugs by using modified Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion technique according to the criteria of the National Committee for Clinical Laboratory Standards (NCCLS). The disks of antimicrobial drugs used were chloramphenicol (30 mug), co-trimoxazole (1.25/23.75 mug), ampicillin (10 mug), ciprofloxacin (5 mug), and ceftriaxone (30 mug). The isolate appeared susceptible to ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone.
The patient was given ciprofloxacin, 500 mg, every 12 hours, orally, on admission but remained febrile after 3 days of treatment. When the blood culture report was received, and in view of the susceptibility pattern, intravenous ciprofloxacin, 200 mg every 12 hours, was administered. Despite 8 days of treatment, his fever did not resolve. The isolate was reviewed and the MIC of ciprofloxacin was determined by Kirby-Bauer broth dilution technique; it was 0.5 mug/mL; well below the NCCLS recommended break point value of 1 mug/mL. However, in light of the treatment failure with ciprofloxacin, intravenous ceftriaxone,1 g every 12 hours, was administered, and the patient responded within 3 days.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 14-year-old boy from Rawalpindi, Pakistan, presented with a 7-day history of high-grade fever (>38 °C) and vomiting.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, previously healthy, was admitted in July 2002 with a 7-day history of high fever (>38 °C) and repeated vomiting.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy; resident of Rawalpindi, Pakistan.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever and vomiting.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, temperature was >38 °C with relative bradycardia (heart rate 84 bpm) and a soft, palpable spleen.
objective.routine_investigations: Total leukocyte count was 3 x 10^9/L. Thin and thick peripheral blood smears were negative for malarial parasites. Routine urinalysis and chest radiographs were normal. Blood Widal test demonstrated an 'O' (somatic) antigen titer of 1:320 against Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi.
objective.advanced_workup: Modified Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion susceptibility testing (NCCLS criteria) of the blood culture Salmonella Typhi isolate showed resistance to conventional first-line antityphoid drugs (chloramphenicol 30 µg, co-trimoxazole 1.25/23.75 µg, and ampicillin 10 µg) and apparent disk susceptibility to ciprofloxacin (5 µg) and ceftriaxone (30 µg). Subsequent broth dilution testing determined a ciprofloxacin MIC of 0.5 µg/mL (below the contemporary NCCLS breakpoint of 1 µg/mL, but indicative of reduced fluoroquinolone susceptibility).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Multidrug-resistant Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi typhoid fever with in vivo ciprofloxacin treatment failure due to reduced fluoroquinolone susceptibility (ciprofloxacin MIC 0.5 µg/mL), confirmed by blood culture, Widal serology (1:320), and MIC testing. Malaria was ruled out on thick and thin blood smears. Initial treatment with oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 12 hours for 3 days followed by intravenous ciprofloxacin 200 mg every 12 hours for an additional 5 days (8 days total) failed to resolve his fever. Upon switching to intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g every 12 hours, the patient defervesced and responded clinically within 3 days.
